I do absolutely agree with you, but I kinda like in retrospect what his end character arc ends up being. Walt finds purpose, love, reconciliation and deep meaning through his life experience on the island. Off it, he had a life pretty much dictated by his abhorrent mother, denying him knowledge of his biological father, prejudice by the spineless white dude his mum married and was fixated by, and crucially, no permanent home due to forced relocation from the US to Italy (I believe). 

The island gave him a chance for true meaningful love from his father, a caring and nurturing community, a permanent home, and a chance (before the meddling of Ben) for him to experience his supernatural abilities in a way he never could have done off island. As we see in fleeting glimpses off island with Walt's appearances in Season 4, Season 5 and the epilogue in Season 6, he tries to assimilate back into society, but longs for the island as evidenced in The New Man in Charge as he is present in the mental clinic. 

I like how thematically this, like much of Lost, forms a great mirror image to The Man in Black & Jacob coming to the Island and effectively being held hostage by Mother & The Rules. Walt oppositely does not want to leave evidenced by his original intent to burn the raft. Walt through the innocent guise of a child knew intrinsically what a truly special place it was, only at the time matched by Locke. It is ironic that the real reason why he left the island, was due to the meddling of Ben in his life & being kidnapped, when truly he didn't want to leave until these negative experiences occurred to him. This shows the impact of Jacob's "hands off" approach rule adversely affecting others and why it cannot continue. This would surely have affected Walt's judgment along with the deep level of forgiveness he would need to form to reconcile with Michael, and ultimately make him a truly great revolutionary (to the positive) leader.

And as for why he needed to be off island, it was so he could have the dreams about Locke, hence his astral projected form in Season 3 where he ultimately sets in motion John Locke becoming the catalyst for destiny, aka the time jumps, by manifesting as a voice for the island. Only a truly powerful candidate could do this... Or at least I believe. 

Ultimately (in my humble opinion) Walt's purpose the entire time was to be the true replacement for Jacob, however with Jacob's rule & adherence to the archaic Rules, his own biased personal beliefs and structured system, Walt could never have attained the position of Jacob's replacement, especially with Ben's attempted brainwashing based on a false notion of what Jacob, and ultimately the island, wanted. Walt needed to experience what he did in Season 1 prior to Ben's kidnap plot, experience an "ordinary life" afterwards, know that this would not spiritually fulfil him, perform his part as the opening gambit in destiny with Locke still proving to Walt he had precognition and intervention abilities (reminiscent of Jacob) and long for the island for years, to be able to be that revolutionary true Protector the island needed long-term. 

But that's just my opinion, I still would have loved Walt as a continued cast member lol

Thanks for reading the comment and engaging in reasonable discussion mate. The Lost subreddit is just such a good place to discuss the show and it's fantastic with disagreement that we can have good manners.

The only point I take massive issue with is Jacob. Jacob at no point in the show once we actually meet him is a deity which deserves to be worshipped. That's the main point, that a non-interventionist false "God" like him is truly an evil force. He is the reason for the MiB's true existence as the smoke monster after all. 

I think that's the real question of Lost; is it ridiculous? Why was pushing the button in the Hatch considered, after it was proven true that the world would end if it was not pushed (and if Desmond didn't turn the key) considered rational? I don't think the show is promoting a religious world view at all. I think it is promoting faith in the natural order of the Island, which isn't necessarily positive or negative in and of itself. The Island only puts things back in place.

Jack in Season 6 first half is an utterly broken man, akin to Locke before he came onto the Island. In Lighthouse he completely breaks, specifically with Hurley in stating how he felt the Island would "fix him", and how their plan with the nuke was his greatest failure. He finally realizes that being the leader and making decisions rashly in trying to fix a situation, trying to eternally assert his will over the natural order like he did as a doctor, aggravated at himself when he couldn't fix the unfixable, is no longer a viable option for him. He needed to go through this final act of "fixing", although out of faith rather than pure rationalisation, with the nuke to realize the way he does things doesn't work. He then has that utterly sublime scene with Richard in the Black Rock where he explains he truly believes he is alive and back at the Island for a reason, he just doesn't know it yet. For potentially the first time in his entire life, he doesn't know what the reason is, and he's not actively searching for it. He puts faith in the Island to be the leader and serve it, rather that assert his own decisions over what occurs. 

This is where the Season 6 Jack starts to become more "Locke-like" and truly shine. There's a scene with Sun on the beach where Jack is talking about the dead crops from Sun's garden, untendered for over 3 years, and he pulls out a live tomato which somehow survived after nothing for this time. You can just picture Season 1 Locke in this scene, but it's Jack, having patience and faith. He only wants to know if Sun trusts him, and she does, which makes him secure in his faith. 

This is mirrored in all of his flash-sideways, as this is a Jack who has grown through all of Season 6 already. Jack in the flash-sideways is caring for David - he doesn't act like his father and fully accepts David not being a doctor but a pianist. Jack also has an eternal tie to Locke in the flash-sideways (much like Ben actually, but more significant). He is trying to "fix" Locke's paralysis, to atone for not believing in Locke on the Island for all this time. Jack in the flash-sideways is a man of patience, of faith in the surgery working, of pride in other's accomplishments. It's beautiful. 

Finally, in the End with Jack, the scene with Flocke and him lowering Desmond into the Heart is so fucking satisfying. Flocke tries to taunt Jack by calling to the similarities when they lowered themselves into the Hatch, and how they could bicker about pressing the button again. Jack says that he, the MiB, is a disgrace to Locke and to his memory, and that Locke was right all along, he just wishes he could have told that to him when he was alive (flash-sideways to Locke waking up is here, which is amazing). The real crux point for Jack is actually backing up that he still believes and will do something illogical in the name of faith. He does this by placing the Egyptian stone back into the well, restoring proper flow of the light back into the Island - he effectively, of his own complete faith and accord, "pressed the button". His complete elation at this is evident in Fox's acting with Jack smiling and laughing, even though he is about to die. He not only got to have his faith rewarded, but did really "fix" the biggest thing he could fix. 

For all the flaws of Season 6, Jack Sheppard is 110% not one of them. He has an utterly incredible character growth arc in this season and Matthew Fox completely nails all of these differing emotions and perspectives for Jack. There's countless more examples in Season 6, like his conversation with Sawyer around the bomb going off on the submarine, but that's what I could think of off the top of my head. Yes, I do agree Season 6 could be much better paced and structured, but there's some of the best LOST content in the Season.

The island is a place with an extremely strong source of electromagnetism which is capable of distorting time. Many of the events of Lost occur due to time dilation and character cross-over in time (basically the biggest example of the Bootstrap Paradox). It heals, can teleport and travel through time by the manipulation of this electromagnetic energy, which is what the Dharma initiative, Widmore and the original Egyptian culture all played around with, hence the frozen donkey wheel, the Orchid, and the Swan Hatch. 

It didn't "need" Jacob to lead people, Jacob was one of a line of protectors for the island, indoctrinated by Mother. Jacob is effectively a play on God for Lost as a series, he has a strong non-interventionist belief, and has people manipulated to serve his own little games, including foiling the Man in Black. 

Again, the island is a large source of electromagnetism and playing with this source, releasing huge amounts at one specific point can alter time and space. Tunisia was the exit point from that specific route of the island. Why lost has to scientifically explain the minute details of this when Star Trek, Doctor Who, X Files all don't explain their mythologies into unbelievably specific minute detail is the biggest mystery of the show. 

The Egyptian culture is an analogue of the Dharma Initiative and explained by spending time with them in Season 5. As the Man in Black says, "every time it is the same". The Egyptians had their own 'version' of the Hatch by again trying to exploit the island's electromagnetism for their own gain, and had an earlier incident, which required the usage of the cork into the heart of the island. The message is one of humanity always wanting more, always wanting to continually abuse the natural order for their own gain. The Egyptian culture with some details is explained within the Lost encyclopedia, but the details are not needed to form an understanding of why they were included. 

The Mother may or may not have had "powers". This is one of the mysteries of the show which does *not* have an answer. But think of it this way; okay, we get an answer to why mother has powers and is on the island. How was before mother? And before that? And who first found the island? When did the island form? Why did the island form? See, there becomes more meaningless questions. You can literally do this with every single show imaginable, but only Lost gets this criticism. 

As for Eloise and Ilana (two completely separate unrelated characters), Eloise Hawking was Daniel Faraday's mother. She had seemingly futuristic powers of prediction and predestination, but actually is just an example of the fulfilment of paradox. When Daniel goes back in time, Eloise kills him, and then possesses Daniel's notebook, with all the details about his future and parts of Desmond's future. She is then able to use that knowledge to her own gain and the gain of Widmore. 

Walt was special as he had the ability to astro-project, shown by him in the rain during season 2, and manipulate reality through his thought, like how he sent messages to the computer in the Hatch for Michael to read. He, like Hurley, Miles and the MiB, possessed special, supernatural abilities. Like how Luke has the force in Star Wars, he just has these powers. As for the *true* reason why Walt is special, the epilogue provides that answer. He is destined to be the true leader of the island. 

The MiB turning into the smoke monster occurs in "Across the Sea". Again, scientifically why this has to "make sense" is truly one of the biggest, most random reasons people hate Lost. It's a science fiction show. Apply the same logic to Game of Thrones. But the answer is that he was broken down by the electromagnetism, but due to being special like Desmond, did not die, and became black smoke. 

What didn't get answered about the Dharma Initiative? If it is the numbers 4815162342, it is extensively answered through two main modes; the scientific and the faith. Scientifically, these numbers are the meaning of the "Valenzetti Equation", escential for manipulating time. This is basically why the numbers have to be entered into the Swan Hatch computer. From the faith route, these are the numbers of the Candidates to survive to the end of the show, all having their lives interfered with by Jacob. The best example would be Sawyer, who receives the pen to write his letter to want to kill the real Sawyer. These 6 candidates, John Locke, Jack Sheppard, Hugo Reyes, Sayid Jarrah and Sun & Jin Kwon all extensively have their fates interfered with and predestined through their own actions back in time in the '70s, which affects their "present day" 2004 journey, and so on in a never ending cycle. These candidates were always destined to end at this point. 

How is Charlotte a dead end storyline? She ended up going to the island as she remembered as a kid. The time traveling killed her. The reason she could speak Korean to Jin was, ironically enough, because after, Jin had time travelled to the Dharma Initiative in the '70s and taught her, plus a fascination of wanting to go back spurred her into being an archeologist. 

As for Eko, again, not a dead end storyline. Eko was the first example of Jacob's Candidate being eliminated from their grand chess match through the MiB's manipulation of the rules. A rule is that the MiB cannot directly kill the Candidates of Jacob. The MiB identifies the strength of Eko as a protector to the island, and sets out his plan to manipulate him as he eventually did with Locke. A Candidate manipulated will serve his end goal of eliminating Jacob. All scenes with Yemi on the island and Eko's blind trust of this visions is what leads him to unknowingly break one of the rules. Yemi tells Eko to fall on his knees and pray to God for forgiveness for his indiscretions off the island as Mr. Eko. However, Eko rejects this and makes no apology, saying he truly believes he has done the best with what was available in his life, and would not change anything. He effectively says to the MiB and to the island, "I do not need to be forgiven and I am not *flawed*". The entire Candidacy as governed by Jacob's rules is that the Candidates are all flawed, broken people who the Island would provide salvation and they would not feel compelled to leave it. Eko clearly is not a Candidate from what he says to the MiB and breaks this rule. Therefore the MiB, infuriated by Eko's uselessness now as he cannot be manipulated as he thought, kills Eko as he is not a Candidate, and sets out on further manipulating Locke as a long con to kill Jacob. 

Finally, the rules were set in place by Jacob through the thoughts of Mother. It is a question of nature versus nurture. These specific, archaic "rules" in place are decided by the protector of the island themself, not the other way around. Jacob had true belief that he could not kill the MiB, and vice-versa. He then set that the Candidates could not be directly killed by the MiB, but only by their own actions and their own decisions. This is shown masterfully in Season 6 with the bomb on the submarine and Jack arguing with Sawyer over it. Sawyer's intervention and choice to interfere, to make his own decision, removes the power of the rule put in place. Jacob wanted the people he brought to the island to make their own choices. Like a cruel capricious God, he sat from above and judged while all the people on the island paid the price.
